strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing a critical bottleneck in end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving: cross-domain generalization, long-tail event handling, and data-efficient domain adaptation without relying on computationally prohibitive multi-modal LLMs.

The formulation of a Gaussian Process (GP) over ego and agent latent tokens paired with a trajectory codebook provides both a structured prior and an interpretable uncertainty estimate, which elegantly connects representation learning, trajectory prediction, and active learning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering diverse settings: in-domain performance on standard benchmarks, cross-city domain transfer (Boston vs. Singapore), unsupervised domain adaptation, uncertainty-guided active learning, and robustness against visual corruptions (low-light, motion blur).

Flexible deployment paradigm: RoCA can serve purely as an auxiliary teacher/regularizer during training (incurring zero latency overhead at inference time) or as an active inference module for enhanced probabilistic planning.
The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and supported by informative ablations, qualitative visualizations, and detailed algorithmic descriptions.
weaknesses: Evaluations are restricted entirely to open-loop metrics on nuScenes (L2 trajectory error and collision rate). As extensively documented in autonomous driving literature, open-loop trajectory evaluation does not always correlate well with closed-loop reactive driving safety and collision avoidance. Incorporating closed-loop evaluation (e.g., in CARLA or Bench2Drive) would substantially strengthen the claims.

Cross-domain validation is limited to cross-city splits within a single dataset (nuScenes Boston vs. Singapore) and synthetic corruptions. Because camera intrinsic/extrinsic setups and data collection protocols are identical across these cities, evaluating true cross-dataset/cross-sensor transfer (e.g., nuScenes to Waymo Open Dataset or Argoverse 2) is missing.

The GP formulation in Section 3.2 is somewhat loosely specified mathematically. The model operates over a finite set of $C=64$ learnable basis tokens per cluster, effectively behaving as kernel ridge regression or Gaussian process regression with pseudo-inputs, yet equations (1)–(4) mix joint token distributions and regression targets without clearly establishing the underlying function prior.

Minor notations and typographical inconsistencies in the loss formulations: in Eq. (4), the term $\kappa(e, B_{c_e,w})$ introduces an undefined symbol $B_{c_e,w}$; in Eq. (5), the sign preceding $\frac{1}{\sigma_{w,a}^2}\mathcal{L}_{motion}$ is negative, which is inconsistent with standard negative log-likelihood minimization.

Multi-stage training procedure introduces practical complexity: training requires sequentially pre-training the base planner, optimizing the basis tokens/GP parameters with frozen planner representations, and subsequently fine-tuning the base planner under distillation/regularization loss.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Addressing cross-domain generalization and sample-efficient domain adaptation is a critical hurdle for deploying end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models in the real world.

Principled and flexible framework: The formulation combining a codebook of basis tokens/trajectories with a Gaussian Process (GP) provides both a robust inductive bias and well-calibrated predictive uncertainty. Importantly, RoCA can serve purely as a training-time regularizer/teacher (incurring zero runtime overhead during standard inference) or as an active GP predictor at test time.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper thoroughly investigates multiple aspects of cross-domain driving, including cross-city transfer (Boston <-> Singapore), robustness against visual corruptions (motion blur, low light), active learning sample selection, and challenging long-tail maneuvers, demonstrating solid and consistent gains over baselines (SparseDrive and VAD).

Detailed analysis and transparency: The appendix provides useful practical details, including pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), an inference latency and parameter overhead breakdown, component ablations, and comparisons under standardized benchmarking protocols.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to open-loop nuScenes: While Boston and Singapore present distinct road topologies and driving sides (left vs. right), they share identical sensor suites, camera characteristics, and vehicle dynamics. Evaluating across different datasets (e.g., nuScenes to Waymo) or in closed-loop simulators (such as CARLA or bench2drive) would substantially strengthen the claims regarding real-world cross-domain robustness.

Notation and mathematical formulation clarity: In Eq. (1) and (2), conditioning a single feature vector $e$ on a matrix of basis embeddings $B_{c_e}$ under a standard GP framework could be explained with greater mathematical rigor (e.g., explicit tensor/vector shapes, multi-output GP assumptions vs. independent channel kernels). Additionally, there is a minor typo in Eq. (4) where $B_{c_e,w}$ appears in the variance formulation without prior definition.

Codebook capacity and coverage: The method relies on pre-clustering human driving trajectories into a fixed number of anchor groups ($N_{code} \times C$). While effective for typical maneuvers, it remains unclear how well this discrete codebook generalizes to extreme or out-of-distribution collision-avoidance trajectories that deviate substantially from clustered human driving priors.

Baseline scope in active learning: In Section 4.5 and Table 3, the uncertainty-guided sampling is only compared against random sampling. Comparing with established uncertainty estimation baselines (such as MC-Dropout, ensemble variance, or classification entropy from the anchor head) would better isolate the specific benefit of the GP predictive variance.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in end-to-end autonomous driving: generalizability and domain adaptation across diverse operational environments without reliance on computationally prohibitive large multimodal models.

The formulation of a Gaussian Process (GP) codebook over ego and agent tokens offers an elegant mechanism to estimate predictive uncertainty, which is effectively leveraged for active learning data selection and variance-weighted distillation.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple dimensions on nuScenes, including standardized evaluation protocols, cross-city transfer (Boston to/from Singapore), visual corruptions (motion blur and low light), and long-tail safety-critical scenarios.

Demonstrates compatibility and consistent gains across two distinct recent E2E driving architectures (VAD and SparseDrive), both in a zero-inference-overhead distillation mode and an explicit GP-inference mode.
weaknesses: The cross-domain evaluation is limited exclusively to splits within the nuScenes dataset (Boston vs. Singapore). Both cities share identical sensor rigs and data collection protocols; evaluating cross-dataset generalization (e.g., nuScenes to Waymo Open Dataset or Argoverse 2) is needed to substantiate true cross-domain robustness.

Evaluation is confined strictly to open-loop waypoint prediction and bounding-box collision checks. As established in recent autonomous driving literature, open-loop metrics on fixed logs can suffer from causal confusion and do not reliably correlate with closed-loop reactive driving performance (e.g., in CARLA or Bench2Drive).

Missing standard domain adaptation baselines: While RoCA is compared against direct fine-tuning, the paper lacks comparisons against established visual or feature-level domain adaptation techniques (e.g., adversarial domain alignment, source-free UDA, or entropy minimization) adapted to the E2E driving feature representations.

Mathematical clarity and notation in Section 3.2 require refinement: Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 conflate token reconstruction with standard GP regression conditioning; specifically, treating the query token $e$ simultaneously as conditioning input and reconstruction target under an empirical basis lacks rigorous statistical justification. Additionally, minor notation inconsistencies exist (e.g., $B_{c_e, w}$ in the variance equation of Eq. 4).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving: cross-domain generalization and adaptation across different cities, sim-to-real domain gaps, and visual sensor corruptions.

The formulation of trajectory and token basis codebooks coupled with Gaussian Process (GP) inference is elegant and well-motivated. It provides closed-form predictive distributions and variance estimates that naturally serve as uncertainty-aware regularization.

Flexible deployment: The GP module can either be retained at inference for maximum accuracy or used purely during source-domain training and target-domain adaptation as a teacher/regularizer, incurring zero runtime compute overhead at test time.

Comprehensive experimental campaign across diverse setups: closed-loop simulation on Bench2Drive, sim-to-real transfer to nuScenes, cross-city transfer (Boston <-> Singapore), closed-loop evaluations on NAVSIM and DriveArena, sensor degradation benchmarks, and active learning.
Strong empirical performance: RoCA demonstrates consistent gains across four distinct base architectures (VAD, SSR, SparseDrive, ORION) in both supervised and unsupervised adaptation scenarios.
weaknesses: The multi-stage training pipeline (pretrain base model -> learn GP basis tokens and parameters -> finetune base model with GP regularization) introduces extra training pipeline complexity, multiple loss terms, and hyperparameter tuning.

The cross-sensor alignment in the Bench2Drive-to-nuScenes sim-to-real experiments is not sufficiently explained. Since CARLA sensor rigs and nuScenes multi-camera configurations have different intrinsics, extrinsics, and field-of-view setups, the manuscript should explicitly detail how sensor discrepancies were handled across domains.

The notation in Eq. (7) for the KL-divergence terms $D_{KL}(c_{pred, e} \parallel c_e)$ is slightly ambiguous regarding whether $c_e$ denotes a one-hot vector, hard index, or soft posterior class probability distribution output by the GP classification MLP.

Minor presentation issues: In Section 4.8 of the main paper, Figure 4 is referenced directly as if it appeared in the main text, but it is located in Appendix C (page 18); minor typos such as 'Ltripplet' and 'a uncertainty criterion'.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Autonomous driving models frequently degrade under domain shifts (e.g., sim-to-real, cross-city, sensor variations, and adverse weather), and fine-tuning large vision-language models for AD can be computationally expensive. RoCA addresses this with an efficient, codebook-regularized probabilistic approach.

Comprehensive and multi-faceted experimental validation: The paper evaluates across a wide variety of benchmarks and settings, including closed-loop simulation on Bench2Drive, cross-domain closed-loop transfer on NAVSIM v1 and DriveArena, sim-to-real transfer from Bench2Drive to nuScenes, cross-city transfer (Boston <-> Singapore), and synthetic visual degradations (fog, snow, blur, low light).

Zero-inference-overhead deployment option: When utilized as a source-domain training regularizer (or during domain adaptation via distillation), RoCA improves the underlying base planner without modifying its inference architecture or introducing runtime latency during deployment.

Effective uncertainty-guided active learning: The GP predictive variance provides a natural and well-calibrated acquisition metric for active learning, outperforming standard heuristics (random selection) as well as established uncertainty baselines (MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles).
weaknesses: Mathematical clarity in the GP formulation: In Section 3.2.2, Equation (2) and Equation (3) formulate a GP over high-dimensional vector embeddings $e \in \mathbb{R}^D$ and the codebook $B_{c_e} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times D}$. In standard GP regression, GPs model scalar functions over input spaces. Reconstructing $e$ from $e$ using kernel evaluation $\kappa(e, B_{c_e})$ functions like kernel smoothing / Nadaraya-Watson regression rather than a rigorous vector-valued Gaussian process; the authors should clarify the assumptions (e.g., independent GP priors across latent embedding channels).

Dependency on discrete cluster classification: Trajectory inference conditions on a hard cluster assignment $c_e = \mathrm{argmax}\, \mathrm{MLP}(\kappa(e, B))$. If an out-of-distribution observation is assigned to an incorrect behavioral cluster (e.g., classifying a soft turn as straight), the GP conditioning is restricted only to the subset $B_{c_e}$ and $W_{c_e}$. The paper lacks an analysis of model sensitivity to cluster misclassifications under heavy domain shift.

Generalization of the source trajectory codebook: The basis trajectories $\{W_k\}$ are sampled and clustered from source domain training data (e.g., nuScenes or CARLA). In scenarios with fundamentally different road topologies or opposite driving conventions (e.g., right-hand traffic in Boston vs. left-hand traffic in Singapore), it is not entirely clear whether a purely source-derived codebook is expressive enough without updating the trajectory anchors.

Minor presentation issues and typographical errors: There are several typographical slips throughout the text (e.g., 'applying the same reconstruction process' in Sec 3.2.2; duplicate 'if the the most informative' in Sec 4.7; 'perturbations or noises to tokens to this token' in Sec 4.8; and 'Ltripplet' in Table 11).

strengths: Extensive experimental scope across multiple benchmarks and simulators, including closed-loop testing on Bench2Drive, NAVSIM v1, and DriveArena, as well as open-loop evaluations on nuScenes (cross-city, sim-to-real transfer, and under synthetic sensor corruptions like snow, fog, blur, and low light).
Model-agnostic plug-and-play design that is demonstrated across several contemporary E2E driving backbones (VAD-Tiny, SSR, SparseDrive-S, ORION).
Zero inference-time overhead when deployed as a training-time regularizer, allowing the base motion planner to operate without additional latency during standard deployment.
Interesting motivation to explore Gaussian Process regression and codebook-based trajectory representations for uncertainty modeling and active sample selection in autonomous driving.
weaknesses: Fundamental contradiction regarding uncertainty loss weighting: The manuscript explicitly claims that the GP predictive variance enables RoCA to 'automatically assign greater importance to uncertain or difficult predictions, thereby effectively addressing the training imbalance towards common scenarios and improving performance on critical long-tail events' (Page 2). However, in the actual loss formulations (Eqs. 4, 6, and 7), the error terms are multiplied by 1/sigma^2 (standard heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL). Mathematically, higher uncertainty (larger sigma^2) down-weights the sample error rather than assigning greater importance to it. This direct contradiction between the intuitive narrative and the mathematical loss formulation undermines the paper's core conceptual argument.

Mathematical and notational deficiencies in Section 3: In Eq. (2), the authors write p(e, B_{c_e}) ~ N([e, B_{c_e}]^T, ...), which improperly confuses a probability density function with a random variable and circularly sets the mean vector to the realizations themselves. In Eq. (3), the motivation for fitting a GP from basis tokens to basis tokens to 'reconstruct' an already-available token e is theoretically vague. Furthermore, in Eqs. (6) and (7), the triplet loss Ltpt is written with discrete class indices as arguments (e.g., Ltpt(c_e, cp, cn)), without formally defining the continuous embedding space over which metric margins are computed.

Lack of domain adaptation baselines: Although the paper emphasizes unsupervised domain adaptation (reporting parenthesized zero-label adaptation results in Tables 2, 3, and 5), it compares solely against zero-shot transfer or direct fine-tuning with ground truth. The paper cites several unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) and domain generalization approaches (e.g., AdapTraj, transfer kernel learning, and adversarial domain adaptation), but does not benchmark against any established UDA or feature-alignment baseline.

Training schedule confounding: In Section A.3, the training pipeline for RoCA involves 48 epochs of base model training, 6 epochs of GP training, and 20 additional epochs of fine-tuning with RoCA regularization (totaling 68 epochs of base model optimization). It is not clarified whether the baseline models were trained for the same total number of gradient updates (68 epochs) to control for extra compute and training duration.

Discrepancy between in-domain ablations and cross-domain gains: In the controlled ablation study on nuScenes (Table 11), the overall gain from full RoCA regularization over the baseline SparseDrive-S is marginal (L2 error drops only from 0.65m to 0.63m, and collision rate from 0.140% to 0.127%). In contrast, other tables report drastic improvements (e.g., Table 1 shows VAD driving score jumping from 42.35 to 56.90, and Table 7 shows route completion nearly doubling on DriveArena). The paper does not provide sufficient ablation or analysis explaining why the regularization provides small gains in-domain but exceptionally large improvements across domains.

Writing and editorial inconsistencies: Section 3.1 contains verbatim repeated sentences ('The GP module contains learned basis tokens, as well as a set of candidate trajectories that one-to-one correspond to the basis tokens. The GP contains learned basis tokens, and for each of the token, there is a matching representative trajectory.'). The main text on page 9 references 'Figure 4', which is located in the Appendix (page 18). Section 4.7 references Section 4.5 for the active learning setup (which is actually the DriveArena section), and Section A.3 cites incorrect equation numbers for the loss functions.
